_meta.description: Vertical explorer — all 13 AI/semiconductor/robotics/optical sub-chains with full step-by-step detail, chokepoint flags, and cross-chain links. Ex-materials (raw materials covered by the Hard Assets map). Fast-moving — enrich over time.

flags.choke: supply chokepoint — concentrated control of a stage

eda.note: The head of every silicon chain — highest-margin, most defensible layer. US duopoly (Synopsys + Cadence) plus Arm IP gate virtually all advanced design. Proven to be a fast on/off geopolitical lever: BIS halted EDA exports to China in May 2025, reversed ~July 2025 in a rare-earth-for-tools trade. China (Empyrean) is far behind on leading-edge full-flow.

chain.d: Synopsys (SNPS), Cadence (CDNS) — US duopoly ~70%+ of design software. Siemens EDA / Mentor (Siemens, SIE.DE) is #3. Export-control flashpoint: US ordered a halt on EDA sales to China May 2025, reversed early July 2025 after US-China trade talks. China domestic: Empyrean (301269.SZ), Primarius (688206.SH) — cannot match full-flow leading-edge coverage.
chain.p: The programs engineers use to draw and check a chip's design — like CAD software, but for billions of transistors.

chain.d: Arm Holdings (ARM) — dominant CPU instruction-set IP (all mobile + growing datacenter via Grace/Graviton); licenses into China via the Arm China JV (a control wrinkle). RISC-V open ISA rising as a license-risk hedge (SiFive private; Alibaba T-Head — China-favored). Interface IP: Synopsys, Cadence, Alphawave (AWE.L).
chain.p: Pre-designed chip building blocks (like a ready-made CPU core) that designers license instead of inventing from scratch.

chain.d: Cadence Palladium, Synopsys ZeBu — hardware emulation boxes; high-margin recurring revenue. Essential to tape out billion-transistor AI accelerators; demand scales with design complexity.
chain.p: Giant machines that test a chip design in simulation before anyone pays to manufacture it — mistakes after this point cost millions.

chain.d: Done in-house by fabless leaders (Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm) and hyperscalers. The high-value front-end where performance is won or lost; increasingly co-optimized with the target foundry process and packaging.
chain.p: The teams deciding what a chip should actually do and how its parts fit together — the architect's job before construction.

chain.r: RTL to mask-ready GDSII; turnkey backend
chain.d: ASIC design-service houses: Broadcom (AVGO), Marvell (MRVL), plus Taiwan turnkey backends Alchip (3661.TW) and GUC / Global Unichip (3443.TW, TSMC-affiliated); Socionext (Japan). Cross-link to Foundry — physical design is co-optimized with the process node.
chain.p: Contractors who take a finished design and prepare it for the factory — the last step before manufacturing starts.

chain.l: Interface IP — SerDes, HBM PHY, UCIe
chain.r: High-speed connectivity IP for AI chips
chain.d: Synopsys, Cadence, Alphawave Semi (AWE.L), Credo (CRDO). HBM PHY + UCIe chiplet-interconnect IP is the new bottleneck for accelerator design as compute disaggregates into chiplets. Astera Labs (ALAB) connectivity silicon adjacent.
chain.p: The specialized connection circuitry that lets AI chips talk to memory and each other at extreme speed.

chain.r: Physical masks transferring design to wafer
chain.d: Photronics (PLAB, US), Toppan (7911.T), DNP — Japan strong. EUV mask blanks: Hoya (7741.T) + AGC near-monopoly (Japan) — a hidden Japanese chokepoint upstream of every leading-edge fab.
chain.p: The physical stencil plates used to print a chip's pattern onto silicon — every design becomes a set of these.

chain.d: EDA + IP sit at the head of Foundry, Memory, Accelerators, Optical and AR-SoC chains. License/royalty model = the most defensible and highest-margin layer of the entire universe; revenue compounds with design starts.
chain.p: Why it matters: every chip in the world, from any company, has to pass through the tools above first.

eda.plain: The design software and licensed chip blueprints every semiconductor starts from — nothing gets built without these tools.

wfe.note: The most concentrated chokepoint in technology. ASML is the sole EUV maker; Zeiss optics + Cymer light source are single-source within it. US+NL+Japan jointly restrict advanced WFE to China. High-NA EUV (~$380M/tool) deploying first at Intel (14A); TSMC is notably holding back, sticking with 0.33-NA EUV + multipatterning for A14/A16.

chain.r: EUV / DUV scanners — the defining chokepoint
chain.d: ASML (ASML, Netherlands) — monopoly on EUV. High-NA EUV (EXE:5200, ~$380M): Intel lead-deployed first unit Dec 2025 for 14A; Samsung receiving for SF2/1.4nm; TSMC holding back (0.33-NA + multipatterning for A14/A16). DUV: ASML, Canon (7751.T), Nikon (7731.T). China SMEE far behind — immersion DUV under trial, sub-10nm scanners unlikely before ~2030.
chain.p: The machines that print chip patterns onto silicon using light — the most complex machines humans build, and only one company makes the best kind.

chain.d: Applied Materials (AMAT, ~18% WFE, broadest portfolio), Lam Research (LRCX — etch/deposition), KLA (KLAC — process control/metrology leader). Japan: Tokyo Electron (8035.T — coat/develop, etch), Screen (7735.T — cleaning), Hitachi High-Tech, Advantest (6857.T — test). Big-5 ~70% of WFE. ALD (atomic-layer deposition) is the gating step for the FinFET→GAAFET (nanosheet) transition — ASM International (ASM.AS) leads, Kokusai Electric (6525.T) on the memory side; Onto Innovation (ONTO) in metrology/packaging inspection.
chain.p: All the other factory machines: ones that add material layer by layer, carve it away, polish it flat, and inspect the result.

chain.r: EUV optics and lasers — single-source sub-chokepoints
chain.d: Carl Zeiss SMT (Germany, ASML-exclusive EUV optics — arguably the hardest-to-replicate component on earth). Light source: Cymer (ASML-owned, US — CO2-laser-pumped tin plasma) + Trumpf (Germany) lasers. No Zeiss + Cymer means no EUV. Pure single-source dependency.
chain.p: The mirrors and lasers inside the printing machines — made by only one or two companies each, so they're hidden bottlenecks.

chain.d: VAT Group (VACN.SW — vacuum valves near-monopoly); MKS Instruments (MKSI); Advanced Energy (AEIS — RF power); Ichor (ICHR), Ultra Clean (UCTT) — subsystems/integration; Horiba (Japan — mass-flow controllers). Many single-source niches inside every tool.
chain.p: The smaller parts inside the machines — vacuum valves, radio-frequency units, precision stages — often from a single supplier.

chain.d: Photoresist chokepoint: JSR, Tokyo Ohka (4186.T), Shin-Etsu, Fujifilm — Japan controls ~80-90% of advanced resist (a deliberate strategic lever). CMP slurry: Fujimi, CMC Materials. Cross-link to industrial gases / specialty materials in the Hard Assets map.
chain.p: The light-sensitive coatings, polishing fluids and special gases fabs consume every day — Japan dominates these quietly.

chain.r: Final integration of the fab tools
chain.d: ASML (Veldhoven NL), AMAT/LRCX (US), TEL/Screen (Japan). Thousands-deep supplier BOM; a single High-NA EUV system ships in dozens of crates and takes months to install — limiting how fast leading-edge capacity can scale.
chain.p: Where the finished machines are physically put together before shipping to a fab.

chain.d: High-margin recurring services + spares (AMAT CSBG, ASML installed-base management) ~30%+ of incumbent revenue — smooths the WFE capex cycle and deepens customer lock-in.
chain.p: Engineers who install the machines in the fab, tune them, and keep them running — a steady service business.

chain.d: China stockpiled DUV ahead of curbs, driving mature-node overcapacity. Localization: NAURA (002371.SZ, ~#8 globally), AMEC (688012.SH — etch), Piotech (deposition) — but supplied <15% of internal demand. Lithography remains the unbridgeable gap.
chain.p: China's effort to build its own versions of these machines after being cut off from buying the best ones.

chain.d: WFE demand = the foundry/memory capex cycle. Buyers: TSMC, Samsung, Intel, Micron, SK Hynix, SMIC. ~$110B+/yr market; China was ~30-40% of spend during the localization rush. Cross-link to Foundry and Memory.
chain.p: Why it matters: the customers are the chip factories — every new fab means billions in orders for these machine makers.

wfe.plain: The machines fabs buy to manufacture chips — lithography, etch, deposition, metrology.

fdy.note: TSMC Fab 18 (Tainan) is the single most strategically important industrial site on earth — ~90% of leading-edge logic. N2 (2nm nanosheet) entered volume production Q4 2025; A16 (backside power) H2 2026. Taiwan concentration is the defining geopolitical risk of the AI era. SMIC caps China at ~7nm (DUV multipatterning) — the central US-China tech-war front.

chain.d: TSMC (2330.TW / TSM) leads: N3 ramping, N2 (nanosheet GAA) volume Q4 2025, A16 (backside power rail) H2 2026; record ~$50-56B 2026 capex. Samsung Foundry (005930.KS) SF2 GAA trailing on yield. Intel (INTC) 18A in production, 14A is its High-NA lead node. A 3-horse leading-edge race; TSMC has ~90%+ of <5nm.
chain.p: Inventing the next generation of smaller, faster transistors — years of R&D before any product ships.

chain.d: Shin-Etsu (4063.T) + SUMCO (3436.T) Japan ~50%+ of 300mm wafers; GlobalWafers (6488.TWO Taiwan, ~17% global), Siltronic (WAF.DE Germany), National Silicon Industry Group / NSIG (688126.SH — China-domestic). Japan/Taiwan chokepoint. Cross-link to silicon / specialty materials in the Hard Assets map.
chain.p: The polished silicon discs everything is built on — a handful of Japanese and Taiwanese firms make nearly all of them.

chain.d: TSMC Fab 18 (Tainan) ~90% of leading-edge; Arizona fabs (N4/N3) ramping for geographic diversification. Samsung (Korea / Taylor TX). Intel (Oregon / Arizona). Taiwan concentration is the single largest tail risk in the AI supply chain.
chain.p: The most advanced chip factories on earth, making AI processors — essentially TSMC, with Samsung and Intel trying to catch up.

chain.r: >16nm: power, analog, MCU, RF, display drivers
chain.d: UMC (2303.TW), GlobalFoundries (GFS), Tower (Israel), Vanguard (5347.TWO). China: SMIC (0981.HK), Hua Hong (1347.HK) — aggressive mature-node build-out raising Western overcapacity/dumping concerns. Display driver ICs and power discretes flow from here into devices and autos.
chain.p: Factories making older, simpler chips that still go into everything — cars, appliances, power electronics.

chain.d: SMIC (0981.HK / 688981.SH) reached 7nm (N+2) without EUV via DUV multipatterning (low yield, high cost) — powers Huawei Ascend/Kirin. Reportedly piloting 5nm (press-sourced, treat as directional) at ~50% higher cost and ~1/3 TSMC yield. US controls cap China at ~7nm with no EUV access.
chain.p: China's best fab making advanced chips with older tools despite sanctions — impressive, expensive, and limited.

chain.r: Customers who design but do not fab
chain.d: Nvidia (NVDA), AMD (AMD), Apple, Qualcomm (QCOM), MediaTek (2454.TW), Broadcom (AVGO) — all depend on TSMC. Fabless + TSMC is the dominant model; IDM (Intel, Samsung) is the alternative. Cross-link to Accelerators.
chain.p: Companies that design chips but own no factories (Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm) — they all queue for the same factory space.

chain.d: Advantest (6857.T) + Teradyne (TER) duopoly in automated test equipment — demand surged with HBM/AI complexity. Probe cards: FormFactor (FORM), MJC (Japan). Yield ramp is the gating economic variable on every new node.
chain.p: Testing each chip on the wafer to see which ones actually work — the yield report card.

chain.d: Leading-edge wafers flow to advanced packaging — increasingly done by TSMC itself (CoWoS/SoIC), blurring the foundry/OSAT line. CoWoS capacity is the gating bottleneck on AI GPU output. Cross-link to Advanced Packaging.
chain.p: Finished wafers moving on to be cut up and packaged — the handoff to the next vertical.

fdy.plain: The factories that physically manufacture chips for the companies that design them.

mem.note: HBM is THE supply gate on AI accelerator shipments — and a Korea-centric chokepoint. SK Hynix leads (~62% HBM, Q2 2025), Micron ~21% (overtook Samsung), Samsung ~17% and clawing back via Nvidia HBM4 qual. All three sold out for 2026. HBM4 (2026) adds a logic base die — pulling TSMC/foundry into the memory stack. China (CXMT, YMTC) years behind but closing on DDR5/NAND.

chain.r: DRAM cell scaling, 3D-NAND layers, HBM stacking
chain.d: DRAM oligopoly: Samsung (005930.KS), SK Hynix (000660.KS), Micron (MU) ~95% of DRAM. NAND adds Kioxia (Japan, ex-Toshiba), SanDisk (SNDK, WD spinoff), YMTC (China). DRAM scaling is slowing — HBM and 3D-DRAM are the frontier.
chain.p: Inventing ways to squeeze more data storage into the same space — the memory equivalent of transistor scaling.

chain.r: Stacked DRAM for AI accelerators — the bottleneck
chain.d: SK Hynix (000660.KS) leads HBM3E (~62% share) and is Nvidia's lead supplier; Micron (MU) ~21% (overtook Samsung); Samsung ~17%, clearing Nvidia HBM4 qual. Each Blackwell GPU carries ~8 HBM stacks. HBM gates GPU output; all suppliers sold out for 2026. HBM4 (2026) integrates a logic base die fabbed at TSMC.
chain.p: Memory chips stacked in towers and placed right next to AI processors — the single most supply-constrained part of the AI boom.

chain.d: Korea (Samsung, SK Hynix) ~70% of DRAM; Micron (US/Taiwan/Japan/Singapore). China's CXMT (ChangXin, private) ramping DDR5-8000 / LPDDR5X — the fastest-growing threat, drawing US Entity-List scrutiny. Server DDR5 demand strong from AI hosts.
chain.p: The factories making standard computer memory — the kind in every server and phone.

chain.d: Samsung, SK Hynix (+Solidigm), Kioxia (Japan), SanDisk (SNDK), Micron, YMTC (China, 200+ layer, Entity-Listed). AI storage tier + enterprise SSD demand. More commoditized and cyclical than DRAM.
chain.p: The factories making storage chips — where your files actually live in an SSD.

chain.r: SSD controllers, CXL, register clock drivers
chain.d: Phison (8299.TW), Silicon Motion (SIMO), Marvell, Microchip — controllers. CXL memory pooling emerging for AI servers. Montage (688008.SH China) DDR5 RCD/register clock drivers — a quiet China-exposed niche.
chain.p: The small chips that manage traffic between memory and processors.

chain.r: TSV stacking, base die, MR-MUF / TC-bonding
chain.d: SK Hynix MR-MUF process advantage; TC-NCF (Samsung/Micron). TSV stacking + hybrid bonding for HBM4. Bonders: BESI (BESI.AS), ASMPT (0522.HK). Cross-link to Advanced Packaging — HBM4 base die fabbed at TSMC pulls foundry into memory.
chain.p: The delicate art of stacking memory chips into towers and gluing them together — where HBM is actually hard to make.

chain.d: DRAM makers + module houses: Kingston (private), ADATA (3260.TW), Smart Modular. Server RDIMM / MRDIMM for AI hosts; MRDIMM is the new high-bandwidth server-memory format.
chain.p: Assembling memory chips onto the sticks and modules that plug into servers.

chain.r: HBM to GPU, DDR5 to servers, NAND to storage
chain.d: HBM into accelerators; DDR5 into datacenter; LPDDR into edge-AI devices; NAND into storage. Memory is ~30%+ of an AI-server BOM and the swing factor in datacenter capex. Cross-link to Accelerators and DC Infrastructure.
chain.p: Why it matters: every AI chip ships with a wall of memory around it — memory demand scales with every GPU sold.

mem.plain: The memory chips that feed data to AI processors — HBM is the AI-critical, supply-constrained kind.

pkg.note: The new Moore's-Law frontier as transistor scaling slows — value migrating from front-end to back-end. TSMC CoWoS is the single gating constraint on Nvidia/AMD AI GPU output; TSMC is doubling capacity yearly and outsourcing overflow to ASE/Amkor/SPIL. ABF substrates (Ibiden/Shinko/Unimicron) and hybrid-bonding tools (BESI) are the secondary chokepoints. Taiwan + China dominate OSAT.

chain.d: TSMC CoWoS (2.5D on silicon interposer) + SoIC (3D) + InFO; Intel Foveros/EMIB; Samsung I-Cube/X-Cube. Chiplet standard: UCIe. Advanced packaging is now ~20%+ of leading-edge device cost and rising.
chain.p: Inventing how to combine multiple chips into one package — the new frontier now that shrinking transistors is getting harder.

chain.r: Interposer hosting GPU + HBM — THE bottleneck
chain.d: TSMC CoWoS is the gating constraint on AI GPU output; TSMC bringing on AP6/AP7 (Chiayi) and outsourcing overflow to ASE, Amkor, SPIL. Rubin Ultra reportedly re-architected over CoWoS-L yield. Panel-level packaging (FOPLP) is the next-gen escape from round-wafer interposer limits.
chain.p: The specific assembly step where an AI processor and its memory get mounted on one base — the #1 bottleneck for AI chip supply today.

chain.d: ASE Technology (3711.TW / ASX — world #1, ~45% of top-10), Amkor (AMKR — Korea-rooted, $7B Arizona fab w/ Apple/TSMC), JCET (600584.SH China #3), Powertech (6239.TW), KYEC (2449.TW — test), Tongfu/TFME (China). Taiwan + China dominate OSAT.
chain.p: Factories you hire to do the final assembly and testing of chips — the outsourcing layer, dominated by Taiwan and China.

chain.r: ABF & BT substrates carrying the package
chain.d: ABF substrate chokepoint (top-5 ~74%): Unimicron (3037.TW, leader ~22%), Ibiden (4062.T), Shinko (6967.T Japan), Nan Ya PCB (8046.TW), AT&S (ATS.VI Austria). Ajinomoto (2802.T) makes the ABF film itself — a hidden near-monopoly. High-layer-count ABF for big AI dies is supply-constrained.
chain.p: The fiberglass-like boards a chip sits on inside its package — an unglamorous part that's been in shortage for years.

chain.d: BE Semiconductor / BESI (BESI.AS) + Applied Materials lead hybrid bonding; ASMPT (0522.HK) bonders; Kulicke & Soffa (KLIC) wire/advanced. Hybrid bonding enables sub-10µm 3D stacking — the equipment chokepoint of advanced packaging.
chain.p: The precision machines that place and bond chips together — a small club of Dutch, Austrian and Singaporean firms.

chain.d: Advantest (6857.T), Teradyne (TER) ATE; OSATs run test floors (KYEC, ASE). HBM/AI complexity lengthens test time and demands known-good-die screening at every stack layer — the hardest test in the industry. MEMS probe cards contacting thousands of 40µm-pitch HBM microbumps are a near-duopoly: FormFactor (FORM) + Micronics Japan. Test handlers + HBM inspection: Cohu (COHU, Neon tool). Burn-in: Aehr Test (AEHR). Nvidia is tightening HBM test standards, adding screening pressure.
chain.p: The final exam: running every finished chip through tests, sometimes for hours, before it ships.

chain.r: Underfill, molding compound, leadframes, bonding wire
chain.d: Resonac (ex-Showa Denko), Henkel, Namics — underfill; Sumitomo Bakelite — molding; leadframes ASMPT, Haesung. Bonding wire links to the precious-metals chain (Hard Assets map). Cross-link to specialty materials.
chain.p: The glues, molds and wires used in assembly — cheap materials, but a few are single-sourced from Japan.

chain.d: Output = finished accelerators/CPUs to system integrators. Back-end is where the AI compute supply chain is most physically constrained today. Cross-link to Accelerators and DC Infrastructure.
chain.p: Why it matters: a finished AI 'chip' is really a package of many chips — this vertical decides how many can ship.

pkg.plain: How finished chips get stacked, wired together and tested — the step where AI silicon is bottlenecked today (CoWoS).

acc.note: Nvidia (~80-90% merchant AI silicon) on a Blackwell→Rubin cadence, defended by CUDA. The structural counter-trend is custom ASICs (Broadcom + Marvell co-design, ~95% of that market) for Google/AWS/Microsoft/Meta/OpenAI — projected to take ~28% of AI servers in 2026. Late-2025 inflection: Gemini 3's success plus Google pivoting to SELL TPUs (to Anthropic, Meta — reportedly for training — and neoclouds via the Fluidstack 'franchise' model) marked the counter-trend going mainstream. The real bottlenecks sit upstream: TSMC CoWoS and SK Hynix HBM — and Google and Nvidia now compete for the same CoWoS, keeping it the rate-limiter. China (Huawei Ascend) is fenced off from both.

chain.d: Nvidia (NVDA) — Hopper→Blackwell (GB200/GB300)→Vera Rubin (HBM4, 2026) cadence; CUDA software moat. AMD (AMD) MI355X shipping, MI400 series (2nm, HBM4) + Helios rack unveiled CES 2026. Intel Gaudi. All fabbed at TSMC; Nvidia ~80-90% of merchant AI training silicon.
chain.p: The companies designing the AI processors themselves — Nvidia's GPUs and their few real challengers.

chain.r: In-house accelerators to cut Nvidia dependence
chain.d: Google TPU (Broadcom-designed; TPU v7 'Trillium' also co-designed with MediaTek 2454.TW), AWS Trainium/Inferentia (Marvell + Alchip 3661.TW), Microsoft Maia (Marvell), Meta MTIA (Broadcom, through 2029), OpenAI (Broadcom, ~2027). GUC (3443.TW) is the backend partner for Google's Axion ARM CPU. Merchant ASIC duo Broadcom (AVGO) + Marvell (MRVL) ~95% of custom co-design; custom shipments projected +44.6% in 2026 (~28% of AI servers). Google is shifting from captive use to selling/renting TPUs (Anthropic, Meta, Fluidstack/neoclouds) — the clearest sign yet the counter-trend is real.
chain.p: Tech giants designing their own AI chips (Google's TPU, Amazon's, OpenAI's) to cut their dependence on Nvidia.

chain.d: Huawei Ascend 910C (SMIC ~7nm, 96GB HBM2e; ~1/3 B200 BF16) — ~600K-unit 2026 target but realistically <300K given HBM scarcity (TSMC die-bank via Sophgo now exhausted). Cambricon (688256.SH), Biren, Moore Threads. China compute self-sufficiency is a national priority.
chain.p: China's homegrown AI chips, built under sanctions — behind on performance but improving and heavily funded.

chain.d: Every leading accelerator = TSMC leading-edge logic + CoWoS packaging + HBM. Designers are fabless; the true gates are upstream — TSMC CoWoS and SK Hynix HBM. Cross-link to Foundry, Packaging and Memory.
chain.p: The catch: everyone above still needs TSMC to build the chip and Korea to supply the memory — design is not supply.

chain.r: GPU board, SXM module, OAM baseboard
chain.d: Nvidia SXM modules + GB200 superchip; HGX/MGX baseboards built by Taiwan ODMs (Foxconn 2317.TW, Quanta 2382.TW, Wistron). Astera Labs (ALAB) retimers on board. OAM is the open accelerator module standard for non-Nvidia silicon.
chain.p: Mounting the AI chip onto the boards and modules that slot into servers.

chain.d: Nvidia DGX; NVL72 rack-scale (72 liquid-cooled GPUs) is the new unit of AI compute. Built by Super Micro (SMCI), Dell (DELL), HPE and Taiwan ODMs. Cross-link to DC Infrastructure and Networking.
chain.p: The full AI server or rack — dozens of GPUs wired together into one machine that costs millions.

chain.d: CUDA is Nvidia's deepest moat — 15+ years of libraries. AMD ROCm, OpenAI Triton and hyperscaler stacks chip at it. Inference-optimization software (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) is the fastest-growing layer as workloads shift training→inference.
chain.p: The software layer (Nvidia's CUDA above all) that keeps customers locked in even when rival chips are cheaper.

chain.r: Hyperscalers, AI labs, enterprise, sovereign AI
chain.d: Buyers: Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, xAI, OpenAI, Oracle, plus neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius) and sovereign-AI clouds. ~$300-400B/yr datacenter capex is the demand engine for the whole stack. Cross-link to DC Infrastructure.
chain.p: Why it matters: this is where the AI money lands first — everyone else in the map supplies or serves this layer.

acc.plain: The AI processors themselves — GPUs and custom ASICs — plus the software ecosystems locked around them.

net.note: At 100k+ GPU scale the network gates cluster utilization — 'the network is the computer.' Broadcom is the quiet kingmaker (Tomahawk 6 'Davisson' 102.4 Tb/s, ~$10B AI switch backlog). The battlegrounds: Nvidia's proprietary NVLink scale-up vs open UALink, and InfiniBand vs Ethernet (Ultra Ethernet) scale-out. Signal-integrity silicon (Astera, Credo) is a fast-growing chokepoint at 224G.

chain.d: Broadcom (AVGO) Tomahawk 6 'Davisson' (102.4 Tb/s) + Jericho routing — dominant merchant switch silicon, ~$10B AI switch backlog; Nvidia Spectrum-X; Marvell (MRVL); Cisco Silicon One. Broadcom is the kingmaker of AI networking.
chain.p: The chips inside datacenter switches that direct traffic — a quiet Broadcom stronghold.

chain.d: Nvidia NVLink/NVSwitch — proprietary, high-margin, locks in the GPU fabric. UALink (AMD, Broadcom et al.) is the open challenger. Scale-up bandwidth is the new competitive battleground; Nvidia took a ~$2B stake in Marvell around NVLink Fusion.
chain.p: The ultra-fast wiring that lets GPUs inside one rack act as a single giant chip — Nvidia's NVLink moat.

chain.d: Nvidia Quantum InfiniBand vs Ethernet (Ultra Ethernet Consortium). Ethernet gaining for the largest clusters; Arista (ANET) the Ethernet leader for AI back-end networks; Nvidia pushing Spectrum-X. InfiniBand retains a training-cluster niche.
chain.p: The network connecting racks to racks across the building — where an open standard (Ethernet) fights Nvidia's proprietary one.

chain.d: Astera Labs (ALAB) — Aries PCIe/CXL retimers, Scorpio fabric switches, Taurus AECs; the AI-connectivity pure-play, targeting UALink in 2026. Credo (CRDO) — ZeroFlap active electrical cables dominant top-of-rack. Marvell/Broadcom optical DSPs. Signal integrity is a growing chokepoint.
chain.p: Small chips that keep signals clean over copper cables at extreme speeds — niche parts with big margins.

chain.d: Arista (ANET), Cisco (CSCO), Nvidia, Juniper (now HPE). White-box for hyperscalers built by Taiwan ODMs: Accton (2345.TW), Quanta, Foxconn; Celestica (CLS) ODM networking. White-box is the cost-down path for hyperscale fabrics.
chain.p: The finished network boxes — Arista, Cisco and the white-box makers.

chain.d: Nvidia BlueField DPU + ConnectX NIC; AMD Pensando; Intel IPU. Networking is moving into the server to feed GPUs directly and offload host CPUs — a fast-growing silicon socket.
chain.p: Special network cards that move data straight into GPUs without bothering the main processor.

chain.d: Pluggable optical transceivers today; co-packaged optics (CPO) emerging. Optics is increasingly the power/bandwidth bottleneck of AI networking. Cross-link to Optical & Photonics.
chain.p: The point where electrical networking runs out of steam and light takes over — the bridge to the Optical vertical.

chain.d: Buyers: hyperscalers + neoclouds. Networking is ~10-15% of AI datacenter capex and rising as cluster sizes grow. Network topology and bandwidth directly cap effective compute. Agentic AI is a fresh demand driver — it generates ~25x the traffic of a chatbot (Cisco), ~80% of it 'east-west' (server-to-server); machine-to-machine traffic is forecast to grow from ~10 to ~537 EB/month by 2034 (Nokia), lifting intra-DC + DCI bandwidth beyond lumpy hyperscaler training orders. Cross-link to Accelerators and DC Infrastructure.
chain.p: Why it matters: at 100,000-GPU scale, the network decides whether all those chips actually get used.

net.plain: The switches, optics and interconnects that fuse thousands of AI chips into one giant computer.

dci.note: Taiwan ODMs (Foxconn, Quanta, Wiwynn ~50% of hyperscale AI-server procurement) build the world's AI servers. The binding constraint has shifted from chips to POWER and COOLING: liquid cooling jumps from ~15% (2024) to ~76% of the mix by 2026 (GB200 mandates it), CDU capacity is the cooling bottleneck, and grid access + transformers gate the buildout. The 800V-DC rack transition (Nvidia's 29-member 800VDC alliance) is the next power inflection — wide-bandgap SiC/GaN rises from ~0% to ~64% of rack power BOM as AI 'inherits' the EV/solar power-semi supply chain. Deepest cross-link to the energy supply chain.

chain.d: Taiwan dominates: Foxconn/Hon Hai (2317.TW), Quanta (2382.TW), Wiwynn (6669.TW — ~50% of hyperscale AI-server procurement), Wistron (3231.TW), Inventec (2356.TW), Gigabyte (2376.TW). US: Super Micro (SMCI), Dell (DELL), HPE. Cross-link to Accelerators (rack-scale integration).
chain.p: The Taiwanese firms that physically build the world's AI servers under contract — enormous revenue, thin margins.

chain.d: Delta Electronics (2308.TW — world-leading power supplies), Lite-On (2301.TW), Monolithic Power (MPWR — Nvidia's reference-design VRM incumbent), Vicor (VICR — factorized/vertical power), Renesas (GaN VRMs via Transphorm), Infineon. The 'thousand-amp problem': a Rubin Ultra GPU (~2,500W at ~0.7V) pulls ~3,500A, forcing dozens of multi-phase VRM channels — phase count quadrupled H100→Rubin Ultra. VRM content per GPU is among the fastest-growing semi sockets; PSU lead times stretched.
chain.p: Getting electricity from the wall down to the chip — power supplies and converters, upgraded for power-hungry AI racks.

chain.r: Wide-bandgap silicon for the 800V-DC rack transition
chain.d: The 54V→800V HVDC rack transition (the only path to 600kW+ racks) takes wide-bandgap from ~0% to ~64% of rack power BOM: SiC for the front-end medium-voltage down-conversion, GaN for the high-frequency step-down. AI is 'inheriting' the EV/solar-validated SiC/GaN supply chain just as that demand softens. Pure-plays: Wolfspeed (WOLF — only 200mm + first 300mm SiC), Navitas (NVTS, GaN); broad-line: onsemi (ON), STMicro (STM), Infineon, ROHM, Renesas. Solid-state transformers (SST) — SiC-based, replacing century-old iron-core transformers (18-30mo lead times) — are the upstream inflection: Eaton, ABB, Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova racing for 2027 (private: Heron Power, DG Matrix). Cross-link to the grid/energy chain in the Hard Assets map.
chain.p: A new class of power chips (silicon carbide, gallium nitride) needed as racks shift to 800-volt designs — inherited from the EV industry.

chain.d: Liquid-cooling inflection (~15% 2024 → ~76% of mix by 2026): Vertiv (VRT), Boyd, Asetek (ASTK.OL); Taiwan: Auras (3324.TWO), AVC / Asia Vital Components (3017.TW), Cooler Master. CDU (coolant distribution unit) capacity is the key bottleneck — market ~$1B→$7.7B. GB200 mandates liquid cooling.
chain.p: Water-cooling for chips too hot for fans — cold plates and coolant plumbing, growing at triple digits.

chain.d: Vertiv (VRT), Eaton (ETN), Schneider, ABB, Legrand. Rack densities hitting 100-130kW+ reshape distribution. Transformer + switchgear lead times are multi-year. Cross-link to the grid/electrical chain in the Hard Assets map.
chain.p: The building-level electrical gear: power strips, circuit breakers, backup batteries — boring, essential, sold out.

chain.d: Hyperscaler self-build + colo: Digital Realty (DLR), Equinix (EQIX); developers Vantage, QTS; neoclouds CoreWeave (CRWV). The convexity is interconnect — Equinix Fabric + Digital Realty ServiceFabric (on-demand virtual interconnect); China colo VNET. Prefab modular DC. The constraint is increasingly power-grid access and permitting, not capital.
chain.p: The construction and real-estate layer: who builds and owns the datacenter shells.

chain.r: Gas turbines, nuclear PPA, backup gen
chain.d: Power availability is the #1 constraint on the AI buildout (DCs ~4% of US electricity in 2026). Gas turbines (GE Vernova GEV), behind-the-meter gas, nuclear SMR/PPAs; generators Cummins (CMI), Caterpillar (CAT). The deepest cross-link into the energy supply chain (Hard Assets map).
chain.p: Where the electricity comes from: on-site gas turbines, nuclear power deals, backup generators.

chain.d: DCIM, PUE optimization, GPU scheduling. Nvidia + hyperscaler software stacks. Less directly investable but central to utilization economics and effective cost per token.
chain.p: Software that runs the facility itself — monitoring power, cooling and workloads.

chain.d: Hyperscaler capex (MSFT/GOOGL/AMZN/META) + neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe) + sovereign AI. ~$300-400B/yr is the demand engine for the entire AI hardware stack. Cross-link to Accelerators and Networking.
chain.p: Why it matters: electricity and cooling, not chips, are becoming the binding constraint on AI's growth.

dci.plain: Everything an AI datacenter needs around the silicon: power, cooling, servers, grid connections and electricity.

opt.note: One of the highest-growth AI hardware segments — optics content per GPU is rising sharply (800G→1.6T). The deepest chokepoint is EML lasers (<5 makers; Nvidia committed ~$4B to lock Lumentum + Coherent supply, lead times past 2027). China dominates module assembly (~63% global; InnoLight + Eoptolink ~60% of Nvidia 800G), but US silicon (Marvell/Broadcom DSPs) + lasers capture the value. CPO (TSMC COUPE) is the 2026 inflection.

chain.d: Indium-phosphide and silicon-photonics design. Coherent (COHR), Lumentum (LITE), Marvell (Inphi), Broadcom. Vertically integrated laser/chip makers hold the edge as line rates climb to 1.6T and beyond.
chain.p: The research layer for sending data as light — lasers, light detectors, and light-guiding chips.

chain.d: Fewer than five firms make EMLs at scale: Lumentum (LITE), Coherent (COHR), Mitsubishi Electric (6503.T), Sumitomo (Japan), Broadcom. Nvidia committed ~$4B (~$2B each to Lumentum + Coherent) in 2026 to lock laser supply; EML lead times stretch past 2027 for others. The deepest optical chokepoint.
chain.p: The tiny lasers at the heart of every optical cable — genuinely hard to make well, and demand is exploding.

chain.r: The chip that drives the optics
chain.d: Marvell (MRVL) + Broadcom (AVGO) dominate PAM4 optical DSPs — the brains of a transceiver — moving to 200G/lane. Linear-drive optics (LPO) and CPO threaten to disrupt the DSP socket. This is where US silicon captures value inside China-assembled modules.
chain.p: The chip that converts electrical signals to optical ones and back — a duopoly-ish specialty.

chain.d: China dominates assembly (~63% global): InnoLight (300308.SZ — world #1), Eoptolink (300502.SZ) — together ~60% of Nvidia 800G; Accelink (002281.SZ). Contract manufacturer Fabrinet (FN, Thailand) builds for Nvidia/Cisco/Coherent (first $1B quarter). Module assembly is a quiet China geopolitical exposure.
chain.p: Assembling lasers and chips into the plug-in optical modules datacenters buy by the millions.

chain.r: Optics moved next to the switch/GPU die
chain.d: The 2026 inflection: Nvidia ships commercial CPO in 2026 — Quantum-X (InfiniBand, 1H) + Spectrum-X (Ethernet, 2H, 102.4 Tb/s) on TSMC COUPE silicon-photonics packaging; Broadcom Tomahawk 6 'Davisson' CPO (already shipped 3 generations to Meta). Cuts per-port power ~30W→~9W. TSMC is the silicon-photonics packaging chokepoint. Cross-link to Packaging and Foundry.
chain.p: The next leap: building the optics directly into the switch or GPU package instead of plugging them in — now entering volume production.

chain.d: Pluggables and CPO consume the same upstream, so own the enablers: SOI wafers — Soitec (SOI.PA, ~80%; TSMC COUPE runs on SOI; Shin-Etsu licenses its Smart Cut); III-V epi via MOCVD — AIXTRON (AIXA.DE, 70-90% + >85% GaN) and Veeco (VECO); wafer bonding / photomask cleaning + laser-to-wafer heterogeneous integration — SUSS MicroTec (SMHN.DE, ~90% mask-clean at TSMC); InP fabs/substrates — Nokia (NOK — only vertically-integrated InP fab in the West, ex-Infinera), Sumitomo, Furukawa. The fiber-array unit (FAU) for COUPE: Himax (HIMX, nanoimprint optics blocks) + FOCI (3363.TWO). Pluggable-optics TAM ~$15B (2025) → ~$34B by 2030 (+~$9B CPO). Cross-link to Foundry/Packaging.
chain.p: The hidden picks-and-shovels: the special wafers and one-of-a-kind machines needed to make photonic chips at all.

chain.d: Corning (GLW) fiber + connectivity; US Conec, Senko — connectors; Japan fiber/connector majors Furukawa (5801.T) and Sumitomo Electric (5802.T) — MT/MPO ferrules, rollable-ribbon cable, DFB laser chips and CPO external-light-source (ELS) modules; Taiwan/China cabling. AI clusters need massive intra-DC fiber. Cross-link to fiber-optic glass (materials) in the Hard Assets map.
chain.p: The physical fiber, connectors and cabling that carry the light — more of it per GPU every generation.

chain.r: Optical circuit switching for AI pods
chain.d: Google's MEMS-based OCS in TPU pods cuts network cost/power at scale — Lumentum (LITE) is the OCS system supplier (R300/R64, Project Apollo); the MEMS mirror chips are fabbed by Silex Microsystems (Sai MicroElectronics 300456.SZ), with Huber+Suhner (HUBN.SW) another key player. Google is driving an OCP standard for OCS. A structural alternative to all-electrical fabrics that grows with cluster size.
chain.p: Switches that redirect beams of light directly, without converting back to electricity — Google's quiet advantage.

chain.d: Optics content per GPU is rising sharply (multiple 800G/1.6T ports per accelerator); 800G+ shipments ~24M (2025) → ~63M (2026), AI optical market ~$16.5B→$26B. Google's TPU build-out is a fresh driver — its internal TPU forecast was revised ~2M→~4M units, helping push optical-module demand from ~3M (2025) toward ~20M (2026), with Google alone ~6-10M via TPU v7; the 800G→1.6T transition is being pulled forward. Component beneficiaries: MACOM (MTSI — 200G photodiodes) and SiTime (SITM — MEMS timing, ~$2/module at 1.6T). Buyers: hyperscalers via switch/server vendors. Cross-link to Networking.
chain.p: Why it matters: every jump in AI cluster size means disproportionately more optics — content per GPU keeps rising.

opt.plain: Moving data with light instead of copper — transceivers, lasers, and the co-packaged-optics shift now in volume.

act.note: Humanoids create a new BOM of ~28-40 actuators per robot. The costliest precision parts are chokepoints historically owned by Japan: harmonic/strain-wave reducers (Harmonic Drive 6324.T), cycloidal/RV reducers (Nabtesco ~60% share), planetary roller screws (NSK/THK/GSA). China is aggressively localizing all three to cut cost — Green Harmonic, Sanhua (exclusive Tier-1 Optimus assembler), Inovance — and Tesla Optimus Gen-3 is reportedly ~70% China-sourced.

chain.d: Humanoid programs drive the new BOM (~28-40 actuators/robot): Tesla Optimus, Figure AI, Agility, Apptronik, Boston Dynamics (Hyundai 005380.KS), plus China — Unitree (IPO expected 2026; G1 ~$16K), UBTech (9880.HK), AgiBot, Fourier. Sanhua Intelligent (002050.SZ) and Tuopu Group (601689.SH) are Tier-1 actuator suppliers in Tesla's Optimus 'T-Chain' ($685M Sanhua order Oct 2025). Cross-link to Sensing and Accelerators (the robot brain).
chain.p: The engineered 'muscle units' of a robot — motor, gearbox and sensors packaged into each joint.

chain.r: High-ratio gearing for robot joints — chokepoint
chain.d: Harmonic Drive Systems (6324.T) — Japan's historic near-monopoly in strain-wave reducers, designed into Western humanoids. China localizing fast: Leaderdrive a.k.a. Green Harmonic (绿的谐波 — 688017.SH, Suzhou, STAR-listed; ~25%+ China share, targeting Optimus supply via a 500K-unit/yr plant), Han's (002008.SZ). The reducer is the costliest part of a robot joint.
chain.p: The precision gears in most robot joints — a near-monopoly of two Japanese firms, and the classic robotics chokepoint.

chain.d: Nabtesco (6268.T) ~60% of precision RV reducers for mid-large industrial joints; Sumitomo Heavy (6302.T) Fine Cyclo; Spinea (Timken TKR). China: Shuanghuan Driveline (002472.SZ), Zhongda Leader, Qinchuan. Planetary gearboxes (the cheaper rotary workhorse): Apex Dynamics (4583.TW), Hota (1536.TW), ZD Leader (603667.SH). Japanese dominance here mirrors its strongholds in WFE chemicals and precision optics.
chain.p: The heavy-duty version of those gears for big, strong joints.

chain.r: Linear actuation for limbs — humanoid bottleneck
chain.d: Planetary roller screws are an Optimus-driven bottleneck: GSA (Germany, primary Optimus supplier), NSK (6471.T), THK (6481.T), Rollvis (Swiss), Ewellix (Schaeffler SHA.DE). China second-sourcing: Ningbo Shuanglin (300100.SZ — scaling to ~300K/yr for Optimus), Shanghai Beite (603009.SH — ¥1.85bn roller-screw plant), Hengli Hydraulics (601100.SH), Hangzhou Xinjian, Wuzhou Xinchun (Thailand plant ~2026); SKF (SKFB.SS). Few makers can produce at humanoid volume/cost.
chain.p: The screw mechanisms that turn spinning into pushing — the hardest-to-make part in a humanoid, and its cost bottleneck.

chain.d: Frameless torque motors: Kollmorgen / Allied Motion (now Regal Rexnord RRX), Allient (ALNT), Nidec (6594.T), Moog; Wolong Electric (600580.SH) high-power motors (China). Schaeffler (SHA.DE) sells a full joint module (gear+bearing+motor), courting Figure/Agility. China motion-control: Inovance (300124.SZ — vertically integrating motors, drives, screws for humanoids), Estun (002747.SZ), Leadshine. Inovance is China's motion-control champion scaling into humanoids.
chain.p: The electric motors doing the actual work in each joint.

chain.d: Encoders: Renishaw (RSW.L), Heidenhain (Germany), Nidec-Tosok. Servo drives: Yaskawa (6506.T), Inovance, Estun. Precision encoders and joint torque sensing are an under-appreciated robotics chokepoint enabling compliant control.
chain.p: The electronics telling each motor exactly where it is and how hard it's pushing.

chain.d: The 'Big Four': Fanuc (6954.T), Yaskawa (6506.T) — Japan; ABB (ABBN.SW); KUKA (Midea 000333.SZ — China-owned). Other Japan arm makers: Kawasaki Heavy (7012.T), Seiko Epson (6724.T — #1 SCARA), Denso, Nachi-Fujikoshi. Cobots/AMRs: Universal Robots + MiR (Teradyne TER), Doosan Robotics (454910.KS, Korea). China's Estun (002747.SZ), Inovance, JAKA, Efort rising fast in cobots/industrial — domestic share climbing.
chain.p: The existing industrial-robot giants (arms in car factories) — the incumbent base humanoids build on.

chain.d: Listed: Tesla Optimus (TSLA), Hyundai/Boston Dynamics (005380.KS — Atlas), UBTech (9880.HK), XPeng IRON (XPEV), Xiaomi CyberOne (1810.HK), Rainbow Robotics (277810.KQ — Samsung-backed HUBO). Private leaders: Figure, Agility, Apptronik, Unitree (cost leader; IPO expected 2026), AgiBot, Physical Intelligence, Fourier, 1X. China's vertically integrated, low-cost actuator supply chain is the key competitive variable — Optimus Gen-3 reportedly ~70% China-sourced. Cross-link to Sensing/Vision and the AI compute 'brain'.
chain.p: The companies assembling complete humanoid robots — Tesla's Optimus and its Chinese challengers.

act.plain: The motors, reducers and screws that make robots move — the 'muscles' of the humanoid build-out.

sen.note: The robot 'brain' (Nvidia Jetson Thor, GA 2025) plus embodied-AI foundation models (Nvidia GR00T, Physical Intelligence) link robotics to AI accelerators. Sensing chokepoints: Sony CMOS image sensors (Japan), China-led low-cost lidar (Hesai >1.6M units 2025), and an unsolved gap in force/torque + tactile sensing critical for dexterous manipulation.

chain.r: Edge AI inference for embodied robots
chain.d: Nvidia Jetson Thor (Blackwell, ~2,070 FP4 TFLOPS, GA 2025 — adopted by Unitree, UBTech, AgiBot); Qualcomm robotics; hyperscaler edge. Embodied-AI foundation models: Nvidia GR00T, Physical Intelligence, Skild. The brain links robotics to AI Accelerators.
chain.p: The onboard computer running a robot's AI — Nvidia again, plus a few edge-chip specialists.

chain.d: Image sensors: Sony (6758.T — dominant CMOS), Omnivision (Will Semi 603501.SH), onsemi (ON). Industrial cameras: Cognex (CGNX), Basler, Keyence (6861.T — Japan sensor powerhouse). Sony's sensor lead is a Japanese chokepoint.
chain.p: The industrial eyes: cameras built for machines rather than people — Sony rules the image sensors underneath.

chain.d: China cost leaders: Hesai (HSAI — >1.6M units 2025, Nvidia robotics partner), RoboSense (2498.HK); US: Ouster (OUST), Luminar (LAZR — auto-focused, stressed). Structured-light/ToF depth: Orbbec (688322.SH). Lidar receivers/photodetectors: Hamamatsu (6965.T). China dominates low-cost lidar — a fast-commoditizing layer.
chain.p: Laser-based 3D vision so robots know how far away everything is.

chain.d: 6-axis F/T sensors: ATI (Novanta NOVT), Bota Systems, Sunrise Instruments (China), Keli Sensing (603662.SH — China's largest sensor maker moving into multi-axis torque). Amazon's Vulcan (Universal Robots arm + Teradyne) is the first pick/stow robot with a real sense of touch — proof tactile sensing is arriving. Tactile / e-skin is still an emerging gap (mostly startups). A genuine humanoid bottleneck.
chain.p: The sense of touch: measuring force and pressure so a robot can grip an egg without crushing it — still an unsolved, wide-open market.

chain.d: Bosch (private), TDK InvenSense (6762.T — ICM-42688 widely used in humanoids), STMicro (STM), Analog Devices (ADI). MEMS IMUs ride consumer-electronics scale; balance/locomotion quality depends on them.
chain.p: The inner ear: motion sensors that keep a walking robot balanced.

chain.d: Overlaps Actuators — magnetic/optical encoders (Renishaw, AMS, Heidenhain, Melexis MELE.BR). Joint torque sensing is key to safe, compliant control and is co-designed with the actuator.
chain.p: Tiny sensors in each joint reporting its exact position thousands of times a second.

chain.r: Turning sensor data into world models
chain.d: VSLAM, perception stacks, sim-to-real training (Nvidia Isaac / Omniverse). The software that makes sensing useful — increasingly bundled with the compute platform and the foundation model.
chain.p: The software layer that fuses all the sensors into one picture of the world.

chain.d: Humanoids, AMRs (warehouse), surgical/medical robotics (Intuitive ISRG). Sensing quality gates real-world deployment. Cross-link to Actuators and the AI compute brain.
chain.p: Why it matters: robots only become useful when they can perceive — sensing is the gate on the whole robotics story.

sen.plain: The cameras, force and touch sensors that let robots and machines perceive the physical world.

dsp.note: The make-or-break component for AR glasses: tiny, ultra-bright, high-PPI near-eye displays. No clear winner among microLED (brightest, lowest yield), OLEDoS (premium MR), and LCoS (mature/cheap for waveguides). Sony OLEDoS powers Apple Vision Pro; LCoS (Omnivision/Himax) is inside the Meta Ray-Ban Display; full-color microLED (JBD) is the long-term endgame. Goertek (China) dominates light-engine assembly.

chain.d: The hardest AR bottleneck — tiny, bright, high-PPI displays. Competing tech: microLED (brightest, hardest to make), OLED-on-silicon (OLEDoS), LCoS, laser beam scanning. No clear winner yet; the make-or-break component alongside the waveguide.
chain.p: The race to build screens small and bright enough to sit an inch from your eye — no winner yet.

chain.d: JBD / Jade Bird Display (China — dominant AR microLED, 0.3in monochrome, full-color sampling), Porotech (UK), AUO (2409.TW), Playnitride (Taiwan), ams OSRAM (AMS.SW), Raysolve (China). Mass-transfer/efficiency yield is unsolved — brightest option for daylight AR but lowest yield. Taiwan + China + UK lead.
chain.p: Microscopic LED screens — the brightest, most promising tech, but fiendishly hard to manufacture.

chain.d: Sony (6758.T — Apple Vision Pro supplier; 1.3in 4K, 0.44in FHD panels), BOE (000725.SZ China — ~400K-nit microLED in 2025 portfolio), SeeYa (China), eMagin (Samsung Display). Korea/Japan/China display muscle; powers premium MR headsets.
chain.p: OLED screens shrunk onto silicon chips — today's premium headset displays (Apple Vision Pro uses these).

chain.d: Himax (HIMX — high-contrast LCoS), Omnivision (Will Semi 603501.SH — LCoS panel inside Meta Ray-Ban Display), Compound Photonics, MicroVision (MVIS — laser beam scanning). LCoS is mature and lower-cost for waveguide AR; Himax is a Taiwan-listed pure-play exposure.
chain.p: Older projector technologies still competing where cost matters.

chain.d: The integrated module that injects light into the waveguide. Goertek (002241.SZ) built the Ray-Ban Display projection engine — a key China assembly chokepoint. Miniaturization + efficiency is the system-level challenge.
chain.p: The complete tiny projector: display plus lenses plus lighting, packaged to fit in a glasses arm.

chain.d: Himax (HIMX), Novatek (3034.TW), Raydium (3592.TWO) — Taiwan dominates display driver ICs. Cross-link to Foundry (driver ICs fabbed at UMC/TSMC mature nodes).
chain.p: The driver chips that control these tiny displays.

chain.d: microLED/OLEDoS sit on a CMOS backplane fabbed at foundries (TSMC, UMC, X-Fab). Links the display chain back into the semiconductor stack. Cross-link to Foundry.
chain.p: The silicon wafers these micro-displays are built on — made in regular chip fabs.

chain.d: Apple Vision Pro, Meta Quest, Meta Orion (microLED), smart glasses. Display is the gating cost/quality component. Cross-link to AR Optics & Systems — the waveguide the display feeds.
chain.p: Why it matters: the display is the make-or-break component deciding whether AR glasses ever go mainstream.

dsp.plain: The tiny projectors and micro-displays that would put a screen inside AR glasses — still an open technology race.

arx.note: Getting the image to the eye in a glasses form factor is the second make-or-break problem. Waveguide combiners (Lumus reflective — in the $799 Meta Ray-Ban Display; diffractive Dispelix/DigiLens) suffer low light-efficiency and yield. High-index glass (Schott, Corning, Ohara) and emerging SiC waveguides (index ~2.7, used in Meta Orion) are deep material chokepoints. Qualcomm is the de-facto AR SoC; Goertek/Luxshare (China) dominate assembly.

chain.r: Waveguide vs birdbath vs pancake design
chain.d: How to deliver the image in a glasses form factor: diffractive/reflective waveguides (AR), pancake optics (VR/MR), birdbath (cheaper AR). Waveguide efficiency + manufacturability is the core unsolved AR problem alongside displays.
chain.p: Deciding how to float a digital image over the real world — several competing optical designs, none perfect yet.

chain.r: The lens overlaying digital on the real world
chain.d: Reflective/geometric: Lumus (Israel — inside the $799 Meta Ray-Ban Display, launched Sept 2025). Diffractive: Dispelix (Finland, polymer waveguides w/ Mitsui Chemicals), DigiLens, WaveOptics (Snap-owned), Vuzix (VUZI — OEM maker, acquired ex-Google waveguide lab 2025). Low efficiency, rainbow artifacts and yield make this a deep chokepoint.
chain.p: The see-through lens that bends projected light into your eye — the defining component of true AR glasses.

chain.r: The glass/SiC the waveguide is etched into
chain.d: High-refractive-index glass: Corning (GLW), Schott (Germany — Ray-Ban Display waveguide glass), Ohara (5218.T), Hoya (7741.T). Emerging SiC waveguides (index ~2.7, wide FOV) used in Meta Orion — suppliers Coherent (COHR), SICC / Tianyue (688234.SH); no mature commercial SiC supply chain yet. Cross-link to specialty glass (materials).
chain.p: The exotic high-quality glass those lenses must be made from — very few suppliers on earth.

chain.d: Nanoimprint lithography for surface-relief gratings: EV Group, Canon (nanoimprint), SUSS MicroTec. Wafer-scale waveguide manufacturing yield is the cost gate; overlaps WFE tooling.
chain.p: The nano-scale printing process that etches invisible patterns into the lenses.

chain.d: Qualcomm Snapdragon AR/XR (dominant), Apple silicon, MediaTek. Low-power on-device AI for glasses is the constraint. Qualcomm is the de-facto AR SoC chokepoint. Cross-link to Accelerators / edge AI.
chain.p: The chip that runs the glasses — Qualcomm's stronghold today.

chain.d: Eye-tracking (Tobii), SLAM cameras (Sony sensors), depth, microphones, hand-tracking. The sensor suite drives the context-aware value of smart glasses. Cross-link to Sensing & Vision.
chain.p: The cameras and microphones that let glasses understand where they are and what you're looking at.

chain.d: Meta (Ray-Ban + Orion), Apple (Vision Pro), Google/Samsung (Android XR), Snap Spectacles. China brands: Xreal (~28% video-glasses share), Rokid, INMO, RayNeo (TCL). Assembly: Goertek (002241.SZ), Luxshare (002475.SZ), Pegatron — China dominates device assembly. VR pancake optics: Goertek, Young Optics.
chain.p: The firms assembling finished smart glasses — Meta's Ray-Bans being the breakout.

chain.d: Meta Ray-Ban breakout (audio/camera AI glasses) is the consumer on-ramp toward full AR; enterprise AR (Vuzix, RealWear). Display + waveguide + SoC are the gating chokepoints. Cross-link to Micro-displays.
chain.p: Why it matters: glasses are the bet on what replaces the smartphone — early, speculative, and winner-unclear.

arx.plain: The waveguides, lenses and device layer of smart glasses — the earliest, most speculative theme in the universe.

ais.g: US-dominated; the one vertical with no Asian chokepoint — value sits in network position and installed base, not fabs.
ais.note: The software toll-roads that agentic AI traffic must cross — added in-scope June 2026 (Citrini SOTT): agents generate ~25x the traffic of chatbots, ~80% of it machine-to-machine east-west, and these layers get paid on USAGE, not on per-token price — which makes them immune to the inference-price deflation squeezing GPU renters. The investable edge: network effects and installed bases here are as hard to displace as fabs are in silicon.
ais.plain: The software toll-roads AI agents travel — delivery, communications, identity, monitoring — paid on usage, not tokens.

chain.l: Delivery edge — CDN, caching & agent gateways
chain.r: Where agent traffic first lands on the internet
chain.d: Cloudflare (NET — Workers runtime, zero-trust, pay-per-crawl + x402 agent-payments experiments; the closest thing to an agentic-era gatekeeper), Akamai (AKAM — CDN pivoting to AI compute delivery), Fastly (FSLY — edge compute + semantic caching for repeated agent queries).
chain.p: The delivery networks where AI-agent traffic first hits the internet — they see, cache and charge for that traffic.

chain.r: Voice, SMS and telephony agents use to reach people
chain.d: Twilio (TWLO — CPaaS + Conversation Memory + voice AI), Bandwidth (BAND — owns last-mile PSTN interconnect, the physical phone plumbing), Sinch (SINCH.ST — European CPaaS in agentic catch-up).
chain.p: The phone and messaging rails agents use when they need to reach an actual human.

chain.r: Which agent is this, and what is it allowed to do?
chain.d: SailPoint (SAIL — identity governance extending from employees to AI agents; the unsolved problem of the agentic era), Palo Alto Networks (PANW — security platformization across agent surfaces). The 'agent identity' layer is a genuine supply gap — nobody owns it yet.
chain.p: The unsolved question of the agent era: proving which AI is acting and what it's allowed to do — nobody owns this yet.

chain.r: Watching what autonomous agents actually do in production
chain.d: Datadog (DDOG — observability for agentic workloads), Dynatrace (DT — AI-native monitoring), JFrog (FROG — artifact + model registry: the 'parts inventory' of shipped AI software).
chain.p: The monitoring tools watching what autonomous agents actually do once deployed — the flight recorder for AI software.

chain.r: The phonebook and pipes under machine-to-machine load
chain.d: VeriSign (VRSN — the .com/.net registry monopoly; every agent lookup touches it), A10 Networks (ATEN — carrier-grade NAT + IPv6 transition gear as M2M traffic compounds toward ~537 EB/mo by 2034, per Nokia).
chain.p: The internet's address book and plumbing — obscure, monopoly-like assets that every single agent lookup touches.
